planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Black Knight requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Black Knight forms tight rosettes of thick, pointed leaves in a deep, near-black maroon-purple, among the darkest coloring available in echeveria, with the color deepening further under strong sun and cool temperatures. Bright red, bell-shaped flowers on tall stems provide striking contrast against the near-black foliage in late spring to summer. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and makes an excellent container or rock garden specimen in warm, dry conditions. In zone 9a grow it outdoors in a well-drained bed or pot through the warm season and protect from prolonged winter wet and hard freezes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Afterglow requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Afterglow forms large, open rosettes of broad, powdery leaves in a shimmering lavender-pink to mauve, with an iridescent, almost metallic sheen that shifts subtly with the angle of light, one of the most photographed and admired color effects among ornamental echeveria hybrids. Strong sun and cool nights deepen the pink-purple tones, while more shade keeps the color cooler and grayer. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and makes an excellent container or rock garden specimen in warm, dry conditions. In zone 9a protect from prolonged winter wet and hard freezes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Neon Breakers Echeveria (Ruffled Pink-Blue Wave-Leaf Succulent)

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Neon Breakers requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Neon Breakers is prized for its dramatically ruffled, wavy leaf margins, unlike the smoother-edged leaves of most echeveria, in a shifting blend of blue-grey and pink that intensifies to a brighter rose-pink along the crinkled edges with strong sun and cool weather, resembling a cresting, colorful wave. Its bold, textured leaf form makes it stand out even among other colorful echeveria hybrids in a mixed succulent planting. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and makes an excellent container or rock garden specimen in warm, dry conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Blue Bird requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Blue Bird forms medium-sized rosettes of smooth, powdery blue-grey leaves with pointed tips that blush a soft pink at the edges in strong sun and cool weather, a calmer, more understated color combination than the bolder purple or near-black echeveria hybrids. Its clean, classic rosette form and reliable offsetting habit make it a dependable, easy-care choice for mixed succulent bowls, rock gardens, and border edging. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and makes an excellent container specimen in warm, dry conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Hercules requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade, giving it extra room to reach its full mature size. Hercules is a large-growing echeveria hybrid producing broad, thick, blue-grey rosettes noticeably bigger than most echeveria cultivars, with wavy leaf margins that pick up a bronze-pink blush in strong sun. Its substantial scale makes it a strong focal point or anchor specimen in a succulent bed or large container, rather than a component of a mixed dish garden. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and offsets modestly at the base over time.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Echeveria colorata requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. This species, one of the parents behind many popular echeveria hybrids, forms substantial rosettes of thick, pale chalky-white to blue-green leaves that flush pink-red at the tips in strong sun and cool weather, with a distinctive stiff, upright leaf posture rather than a flat, spreading rosette. Its bold color and sturdy leaf form have made it a favorite species in its own right as well as a foundational parent in echeveria breeding programs. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings, and offsets moderately at the base over time.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant offsets or container stock in spring in well-drained, lean, gritty soil in full sun to part shade; Echeveria pulidonis requires perfect drainage and is intolerant of standing water in the center of the rosette.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean, gritty to sandy soil in full sun to part shade. Echeveria pulidonis is a compact Mexican species forming small, tidy rosettes of thick blue-green leaves crisply edged in bright red, with the red margin intensifying in strong sun and cool weather for sharp two-tone contrast. Bright yellow-orange, bell-shaped flowers appear on short stems in spring, adding seasonal color to the neat foliage rosette. Its small, well-behaved scale and reliable offsetting from the base make it a popular choice for compact succulent dish gardens and collections. Like other echeveria it needs sharp drainage and infrequent, deep watering, letting the soil dry out fully between waterings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
